title: How Costco Really Makes Money
the_thought: The card at the door is the real checkout.
hook: A Costco shopper rolls a flat cart toward the exit lights. The clerk scans a television, a salmon slab, a tower of paper. The receipt is long and loud. But that noisy till is not how Costco really got paid for the year. Why would a warehouse that prints thin prices still report more than ten billion dollars of operating income? Look back at the door. A gold card got scanned on the way in. The year was already sold.

levels.name: Exit Receipt
beats: The exit looks like the whole business. Pallets. Beeps. A paper ribbon that never seems to end. A shopper paid for a week of food and a television in one pass, and the room sounds like a factory that sells groceries. That is the show Costco puts on purpose. The show works because the warehouse is real. Costco is principally a membership warehouse. In fiscal 2025 it reported 269.912 billion dollars of net sales. That is a mountain of chicken, tires, gasoline, and televisions. If you only watch the mountain, you will think the company makes money the way a supermarket makes money. Buy a thing. Mark it up. Keep the difference. Watch the receipt, then ask a ruder question. If the pallets are the product, why is the gross margin so thin that a normal retailer would panic? Costco's fiscal 2025 gross margin was 30.026 billion dollars, or 11.12 percent of net sales. Eleven cents on the dollar before the building, the people, and the lights are paid. That is not a grocery victory lap. That is a tightrope. Merchandise costs in that year were 239.886 billion dollars. Selling, general, and administrative expenses were 24.966 billion dollars. Operating income, after those two giant lines, was 10.383 billion dollars. Net income was 8.099 billion dollars. So the noisy till is huge, and the leftover is still large. The puzzle is which part of the leftover is the pallet, and which part was collected before the cart even rolled. Here is the customer mystery. A person can spend four hundred dollars at the exit and still not have paid for the thing Costco protects most. The exit is public. The door is quiet. Why build a business that hides its best till at the entrance? Costco's own 10-K says the membership format is integral to the business and to profitability. That is not a slogan on a bag. That is a risk factor. If signups stall, if Executive upgrades stall, if renewals crack, net sales and membership fee revenue both get hurt. The mountain of pallets depends on a card you cannot see on the receipt. So the exit is not a lie. It is a decoy. The decoy is loud on purpose. Cheap pallets pull a body through the door. The door is where the year gets sold. If that is true, the next question is simple. How thin are the stickers, really, and why is Costco allowed to print them that way?

levels.name: Thin Stickers
beats: Costco tells members it wants prices that feel consistently lower than elsewhere. The 10-K calls the idea pricing authority. Not a one-day sale. A reputation. That reputation is expensive to keep, because Costco will sometimes hold a price even when its own costs rise. Gross margin takes the hit. The member does not. That is a strange decision unless the pallet is not the whole till. A supermarket that lived only on markup could not keep playing chicken with its own sticker. Costco can, because something else is catching the year. Look at the floor. Costco warehouses are not elaborate. Average space is about 147,000 square feet. Merchandise sits on racks above the sales floor and on pallets in the aisle. The company carries less than 4,000 active stock keeping units in the core warehouse, significantly less than other broadline retailers. Fewer things to count. Fewer things to lose. Faster turns. But why starve the aisle on purpose? Fewer SKUs is not a cute constraint. It is the machine that makes thin stickers possible. A warehouse that tried to be a full supermarket would drown in handling costs. Costco refuses that drowning. The missing aisles are a feature. Treasure-hunt pallets make a member walk the whole floor. Walking the floor is how a thin sticker still produces a fat cart. Gasoline looks like another sticker game. Costco operated 747 gas stations at the end of fiscal 2025. Gasoline was about 10 percent of total net sales that year. The 10-K is clear that gasoline generally has a lower gross margin percentage than the rest of the warehouse, and that it enhances traffic. Cheap gas is not a side hustle. It is a magnet that pulls a car onto the lot, which pulls a body through the door, which pulls a cart down the pallet aisle. Kirkland Signature is the other quiet sticker. Costco says those private-label goods are high quality, generally cheaper than national brands, and generally earn higher margins. But why does a white bottle matter if the door is the till? The company expects to keep raising that penetration. The white bottle is not a mascot. It is how a thin warehouse still finds a fatter inch on some pallets without breaking the cheap-price story. There is one more trick under the sticker, and it is almost rude. Costco often sells inventory before it has to pay the supplier, even while taking early payment discounts. The pallet leaves. The cash sits. Then the bill arrives. That float is not membership. It is the warehouse acting like a brief bank. Combined with thin prices, it means Costco can look generous on the shelf and still keep the lights on. Online is a different shelf. The 10-K says the company averages 9,000 to 10,000 SKUs on its e-commerce sites, some of which are also in the warehouse. That is still not a full internet store. It is the limited-list idea with a bigger catalog, and it still sits on top of the same paid door. You do not browse as a stranger who never bought the year. The website is another aisle for people who already paid to enter. So the stickers are thin on purpose. Ancillary businesses pull traffic. Private label recovers a little margin. The depot system and the pallet display cut handling. But even after all of that, fiscal 2025 operating income was 10.383 billion dollars on 269.912 billion dollars of net sales. The leftover still needs another explanation. If the stickers are the bait, what is sitting at the door?

levels.name: Door Money
beats: Now reverse the trip. Before the salmon, before the television, a gold-toned card hits a scanner at the entrance. Costco calls this the membership format. Gold Star memberships are for individuals. Business memberships are for businesses, with paid affiliates. In the United States the annual fee for those memberships was 65 dollars in the fiscal 2025 10-K, and every paid membership includes a free household card. That is the quiet till. In fiscal 2025, membership fees were 5.323 billion dollars. Total revenue, sales plus those fees, was 275.235 billion dollars. Line the fee against total revenue and it looks tiny, about 1.9 percent. Line the same 5.323 billion against 10.383 billion of operating income and it looks like about half the operating profit, if you simply set the two numbers next to each other. That second ratio is not a fully cost-allocated profit split. The membership desk still uses people and square footage. But it is the cleanest way the filings let you see why the door matters more than the receipt. Membership fee revenue is accounted for on a deferred basis, recognized ratably over the one-year membership period. At the end of fiscal 2025, deferred membership fees were 2.854 billion dollars. That is money already collected for months of door access that have not been used yet. The warehouse has not handed over the chicken. The year is already on the books, waiting to be earned a day at a time. Costco increased annual membership fees in the United States and Canada effective September 1, 2024. The 10-K says that increase accounted for about 40 percent of membership income growth in fiscal 2025. The rest of the growth was new members. Raising the door price did not empty the parking lot. That is a tell. People will argue about a 65 dollar sticker on a television. They will still pay 65 dollars to keep walking through the same door. At the end of fiscal 2025 Costco had 81.0 million paid members and 145.2 million cardholders. But why do they come back? The renewal rate was 92.3 percent in the United States and Canada, and 89.8 percent worldwide. The 10-K warns that online signups renew at a slightly lower rate. Even with that drag, nine out of ten members in the home markets came back. A supermarket does not get a second till that renews like that. By strictly controlling entrances and exits, Costco also believes shrinkage is well below typical retail. The door is not only a fee machine. It is a lock. Random traffic does not wander in, pocket a steak, and wander out. The gold card is a bouncer that pays rent. Pharmacy, optical, hearing aids, tires, and the food court sit next to the pallets on purpose. The 10-K groups them as warehouse ancillary. They are not a mall of random tenants. They are reasons to make a second trip in the same week, which is how a 65 dollar door keeps feeling cheap. A member who only came for a television would renew out of guilt. A member who also fills a prescription and a tank renews out of habit. So the door sells the year, then the aisle sells the week. If members stopped paying for the door, the thin stickers would have nothing to stand on. That is why the 10-K talks about membership loyalty in the same breath as profitability. The strange next question is why so many members pay extra for a second gold layer, and why that layer does 73.6 percent of the sales.

levels.name: Gold Upgrade
beats: Paid members, except affiliates, can upgrade to Executive. In the United States the extra annual fee was another 65 dollars in the fiscal 2025 filing. Executive members earn a 2 percent reward on qualified purchases, generally up to 1,250 dollars a year, redeemable in the warehouse. It looks like Costco is paying you to shop. Why pay people to buy more chicken? Watch the loop. At the end of fiscal 2025, Executive members were 38.7 million of 81.0 million paid members. That is not quite half the paid base. Those Executive members represented about 73.6 percent of worldwide net sales. The smaller card pack is doing most of the pallet work. The 2 percent reward is booked as a reduction of net sales, not as a cute coupon off to the side. For fiscal 2025 the net reduction in sales was 3.007 billion dollars. Set that beside 5.323 billion dollars of membership fees. Costco collected the door, then handed a huge slice back as a sales haircut to the people who spend the most. Why pay your best customers to buy more chicken? Because the upgrade is how the door gets thicker. A household that already shops like a small business will do the math on 2 percent and pay the second 65 dollars. Once they pay it, they have a reason to steer the next television, the next gasoline fill, the next pharmacy run back to the same warehouse. The reward is not charity. It is a magnet glued to the gold card. In the United States, Costco also added exclusive shopping hours for Executive members. That is a small door inside the door. Time of day becomes a perk. The warehouse gets a quieter hour with the people who already spend like a fleet. By the third quarter of fiscal 2026, the 12 weeks ended May 10, 2026, paid members had grown to 82.9 million. Membership fees in that quarter were 1.373 billion dollars on 69.154 billion dollars of net sales. Operating income was 2.815 billion dollars. Renewal rates were still 92.2 percent in the United States and Canada. The door was not a pandemic leftover. It was still the spine. Costco launched the Executive program in China in that quarter and said early adoption was strong. But why export the gold upgrade first? The gold upgrade is the exportable piece of the model. You can copy pallets. Copying a member who will pay twice, then spend three-quarters of the warehouse's sales, is harder. So the gold card is not a color. It is a filter. It sorts the people who treat Costco like a weekly depot from the people who come for a hot sample and a television. The filter makes the thin stickers safer, because the heavy traffic is already prepaid at the door. If this is so simple, why do copycat clubs still fail to feel like the same place?

levels.name: Why Copycats Fail
beats: Walmart's Sam's Club and BJ's Wholesale Club already run membership warehouses in the United States. The 10-K lists them. It also lists Walmart, Target, Kroger, and Amazon as general merchandise competitors. So the idea of a paid door is not a secret. A person can buy a club card somewhere else tomorrow. Why does Costco's door still print those fees? Start with the SKU limit. Less than 4,000 active items in the core warehouse is a discipline most retailers cannot stand. Buyers want more colors. Landlords want more categories. A copycat that adds aisles to look complete slowly becomes a supermarket with a cover charge. Then the cover charge feels like a tax, and the stickers are no longer special. Costco's depots are the other discipline. Most merchandise is bought from suppliers and routed to cross-docking points or straight to warehouses. The 10-K says this creates freight volume and handling efficiencies. A club that cannot fill trucks like that cannot print the same thin sticker, and without the thin sticker the door fee starts to look like a joke. But why copy the box and miss the trucks? Labor is part of the copy problem too. Costco says operating hours are shorter than many retailers, and that labor costs are lower relative to sales volume because of warehouse efficiencies. In fiscal 2025 it employed 341,000 people, about 95 percent in warehouses and distribution. Around 5 percent were represented by unions. The company targets at least half of the base as full-time, and it talks about careers rather than shifts. In the United States and Canada, retention for employees with at least one year on the job was about 94 percent. A copycat can match a pallet rack. Matching a workforce that stays is slower, and turnover is how thin stickers quietly die. But why would a copycat fail the labor test? Net cash from operations was 13.335 billion dollars in fiscal 2025. So what? That cash comes from net sales and membership fees, then goes back out to suppliers, wages, utilities, card processing, leases, and taxes. The 10-K also notes that the gap between inventories and accounts payable moves with turns, supplier terms, and those early-pay discounts. A copycat can print a club flyer. Copying that cash cycle is the unglamorous half of the model. Geography is a quiet moat. U.S. and Canadian operations were 86 percent of net sales and 84 percent of operating income in fiscal 2025. California alone was 26 percent of U.S. net sales. That concentration is also a risk the 10-K spells out. It is still a fact of the machine. A lot of the door money sits in places where the warehouses are already huge and the habit is already old. New warehouses cannibalize old ones. Costco says so. A new building in an existing market steals members from the last building. Square footage growth gets harder as good sites get scarce. That is why comparable sales, not just openings, are what the company calls the most important driver of profitability. Copycats that grow by planting clubs on cheap land still have to win the next trip, not the ribbon cutting. Online memberships are a leak. They renew a little worse. The Q3 fiscal 2026 10-Q repeats the warning. A digital coupon can buy a signup. It cannot buy the habit of steering a minivan to the same gas canopy every week. The door still works best when the warehouse is a place, not a code. Sam's Club can look similar from the parking lot. Same giant box. Same flat cart. Same idea of paying to enter. The difference Costco protects is the combination: brutal SKU limit, depot math, a gold upgrade that owns most of the sales, and a renewal rate in the home markets that still sits above 92 percent. Take one piece out and the thin sticker stops making sense. But the member still bought the year. If the copycats have the box, what is the one object that still belongs to Costco's story?

levels.name: Pay For The Door
beats: The object is the gold card at the door. Not the television. Not the salmon. Not the long receipt. The card at the door is the real checkout. Say it again, because the exit is so loud the sentence is easy to drop. The card at the door is the real checkout. You pay Costco for the year before you pay Costco for the food. The pallets are how the company keeps the card from feeling like a scam. Fiscal 2025 is the clean picture. But why line those numbers up again? Net sales of 269.912 billion dollars at an 11.12 percent gross margin. Membership fees of 5.323 billion dollars sitting next to 10.383 billion dollars of operating income. Eighty-one million paid members. Executive members under half the paid base and about three-quarters of the sales. A 3.007 billion dollar Executive reward haircut that still leaves the door as the high-margin till. Deferred fees of 2.854 billion dollars already in the drawer for months not yet walked. By May 10, 2026, the warehouse count was 928, and paid members were 82.9 million. The door kept adding bodies. The stickers stayed thin enough that the parking lot still filled. The weakness is real. California and Canada concentration. Gasoline mix that can shove gross margin around. Online signups that renew worse. Cannibalization when the next warehouse opens down the road. Competitors who already know how to charge a club fee. None of that is fake danger. It is why Costco talks about renewal rates the way other companies talk about product launches. Co-branded cards and fresh foods helped the fiscal 2025 gross margin, the 10-K says, even as a LIFO charge for higher merchandise costs pulled the other way. Those are inches, not a new business. The inches matter because the stickers are already thin. A bad inch on food is how a warehouse starts looking like every other giant store that charged you to walk in. The real business is still simple enough to tell a child. Costco sells a door. Then it fills a giant room with a short list of things, priced so the door feels smart. The gold card is how you prove you bought the year. The exit receipt is how you prove you used it. That is how Costco really makes money. Not by winning a markup contest on paper towels. By charging for the door, then making the aisle so cheap you forget you already paid. But why does the cousin club still feel different?

Sam's Club will still be there in the next parking lot, running a cousin of the same idea under a different owner. But why does the box still rhyme? The question to take with you is not which logo is on the gas canopy. It is which club sold you the year at the door, and which one is still hoping the receipt will do that job. But why hope the receipt will do that job?
